newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Defiant Major enjoys rebel Euro role.
newsitem.headline: Defiant Major enjoys rebel Euro role.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major, shrugging off a crushing byelection defeat which wiped out his parliamentary majority, this weekend lectured European leaders on jobs and warned of the dangers of rushing into closer union.

In a combative performance at what opinion polls suggest will be his last European summit as premier, Major told his fellow leaders that allowing some states to forge ahead towards political integration could create dangerous instability.

"The right sort of flexibility would ensure...those who do not wish to integrate are not forced into unwished for obligations which are unattractive to their electors, unappealing to them as governments and which build up resentment across Europe.
"The wrong sort of flexibility would blow the European Union wide apart," Major told a news conference.

As leaders overcame a Franco-German dispute to cement a landmark pact on budget discipline taking the 15-nation bloc a significant step closer to a European single currency, Britain was once again in a minority of one on a wide range of issues.
But Major, beset at home by civil war in his ruling party over Europe and with a election looming anytime before May, revelled in his isolation.
"The United Kingdom is perhaps the grit in the European oyster. It may not look pretty from the outside but I can tell you it's very effective from the inside," he said.
Major's defiant performance was as much directed at his fractious members of parliament as his fellow leaders.

Thursday's crushing victory for Labour in a byelection in the northern English mining town of Barnsley has wiped out his majority, although Major said again on Friday he intended to hang on to power. The deadline for the election is May.
But Europe is proving as intractable for Major as it did for his predecessor, Margaret Thatcher, brought down by the party's bitter divisions over Britain's links with the continent.

Labour, more than 20 points ahead of the Conservatives in polls, has taken every opportunity to widen the divisions, forcing "Eurosceptic" Conservatives to demand an even tougher line against Brussels and pushing Major on to the defensive.
Major again outlined in Dublin the list of reforms he will oppose to the end, including more majority voting to break deadlocks and any bigger role for Brussels in employment policy.

For some at the summit, his solitary campaign brought little sympathy. "Nobody reacted," said one minister at the meeting who asked not to be named, commenting on Major's discourse to other leaders on why their employment policies were far too rigid.
With a flash of anger, Major hit back, saying: "I wonder what the employment rate is in that particular minister's country and whether it is going up or down. Ours is going down."

Others had more sympathy. Swedish foreign minister Lena Hjelm-Wallen said: "He made some very personal statements...When he becomes personal like that and explains what people in Britain stand for...it's a more winning style."
His finance minister Kenneth Clarke, whose pro-European stance has caused the government a string of headaches in recent weeks, also weighed in behind Major.

"The Prime Minister made by far the best speech this afternoon and the one that was listened to more than that of any other minister...We are here as one of the big global economies...We actually speak with some clout," Clarke said.
